newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan opens up television to private business.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan opens up television to private business.

text.p: Pakistans caretaker government has ordered television and radio to be opened up to multiple private broadcasters, Information Minister Irshad Ahmed Haqqani said on Saturday.
President Farooq Leghari issued an ordinance on Friday to set up an Electronic Media Regulatory Authority ending private monopolies and opening up the sector, Haqqani told Reuters.
He said the constitution of the authority should not take long but it depended on the new government how quickly they set it up or if they wanted to make any changes.
The caretaker government of Prime Minister Meraj Khalid is expected to hand over power to the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) party on Monday after PML won a landslide in February 3 polls.
Haqqani said the aim of the measure was to broaden the scope well beyond the currently limited number of television and radio broadcasters and encourage competition.
"There should be more channels and people should have a choice of what to watch and listen," he said. "There should be healthy competition and people should strive for the best."
Under the ordinance licences can only be issued to Pakistanis and no company operating under the laws of any foreign government will be given a licence.

Ali Pasha, chief executive of the only privately-owned network Shaheen Pay Television (SPTV), which also runs FM radio stations in major cities, said opening of gates to other private broadcasters was not financially feasible.

"This will choke the industry, any new person will either fail himself or close down somebody else because of the small size of the advertising market," Pasha, whose SPTV was given 10-year exclusive rights in 1995, told Reuters.

Pakistans annual advertising revenue was estimated at 1.5 billion rupees ($37.4 million) and the state-owned Pakistan Television got the biggest share of one billion rupees, Pasha said. He said rest of the revenue was not enough to sustain several broadcasters.
But Haqqani said that fear was misplaced because new people will only come into the industry after looking at the business prospects and doing feasibility studies.
"The principle of survival of the fittest will be implemented here and if somebody thinks he will get advertising, only then will he start," Haqqani added.

SPTV, which has at least 70,000 subscribers, was given a licence to broadcast during the rule of prime minister Benazir Bhutto whose government was dismissed on disputed corruption charges by Leghari in November.
Other groups interested in setting up broadcasting stations at the time took up the matter in the courts challenging the exclusivity rights.
The case is still being heard in the courts, Pasha said.

Several applications from other parties for running private television channels are pending before the government, including one from the Jang group, which publishes the mass-circulation Urdu-language daily Jang, government officials say.
